title: Knowledge check: Data Manipulation with the Tidyverse

questions.prompt: For “Data Manipulation with the Tidyverse”, which approach best supports a reliable result?
options: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
Trust the first output without inspecting its inputs.
Hide warnings and skip validation to make the result look clean.
Change several unrelated parts at once so the cause of any result is unclear.
questions.answer_key: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
questions.explanation: Data Manipulation with the Tidyverse is one step in Data Cleaning and Manipulation; a tidy workflow keeps variables, observations and values well-defined and verifies joins and row counts. Reliable work makes assumptions visible and checks behavior before scaling up.

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Data Manipulation with the Tidyverse” in the source curriculum?
options: Change unrelated settings before checking the input
Assume one example proves every edge case
Skip validation when the output looks plausible
questions.explanation: The source PDF lists “Introduction to dplyr” as part of lesson 115. The lesson retains the original topic wording.

questions.prompt: When applying “Data Manipulation with the Tidyverse” to real work, what should you do before relying on the result?
options: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
Assume missing and malformed inputs never occur.
Use the same method regardless of data type or the research question.
Remove inconvenient observations without recording the decision.
questions.answer_key: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
questions.explanation: Document missing-value, duplicate, outlier and type-conversion decisions before interpreting results. Record assumptions and known limitations instead of presenting a demonstration as proof.
